title: Deepfakes Are Dominating Global Elections, and Regulation Is Playing Catch-Up
gist: CSIS analysts show AI deepfakes went mainstream in 2026 elections (Brazil, Israel, Spain, Colombia, US midterms with $137M on AI videos, 70% undisclosed) while regulation struggles on three fronts—defining deepfakes (Brazil's TSE narrowed its ban 5–2), separating expression from deception (labels give cover), and enforcing at viral speed; the US has only a state patchwork.

insights.claim: Lula won an unprecedented fourth term as Brazil's president on October 25, 2026, defeating Flávio Bolsonaro in a campaign the authors say was defined by the state's ability to keep pace with AI-generated content.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Brazil's political continuity is set; the deepfake fight is the template for other elections.
insights.quote: Lula secured an unprecedented fourth term
insights.locator: This round of Brazil’s electoral battle

insights.claim: Jair Bolsonaro, under house arrest and barred from public statements, endorsed his son Flávio's presidential bid at a July party convention via a 46-second AI avatar video that disclosed its AI origins; his representative denied authorizing it.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: AI avatars let legally silenced politicians campaign—a new vector regulators must address.

insights.claim: Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) ruled 5–2 to narrow its 2024 deepfake ban to content with 'a degree of realism or verisimilitude' that qualifies as 'electoral propaganda,' so the Bolsonaro avatar shown at a closed convention was not covered.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Broad AI bans tend to get narrowed under high-stakes pressure—expect weaker enforcement than headline rules suggest.
insights.quote: a degree of realism or verisimilitude
insights.locator: By design, the ban was broad.

insights.claim: Brazil's 2024 TSE rule had banned political deepfakes outright—any synthetic likeness, even with consent—plus required AI labeling, making it among the broadest such rules.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Benchmark for the strict end of the deepfake regulation spectrum.
insights.quote: The prohibition applied even with an individual’s consent.

insights.claim: The authors argue Brazil's narrowed rule is more precise but significantly harder to apply, since courts must decide case by case and often after dissemination whether content is 'electoral propaganda' and then weigh 'realism.'
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Case-by-case post-hoc enforcement means deepfakes circulate before rulings—limited deterrent effect.
insights.quote: What Brazil now has is a rule that is more precise but significantly harder to apply.

insights.claim: Brazil's experience suggests deepfake bans are easy to write but, when applied to high-stakes elections and leading national candidates, may yield political and legal caution that undermines their goal.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk to AI/platform firms from election bans may be overstated in practice.
insights.quote: Deepfake bans are easy to write in principle

insights.claim: Brazil's deepfake rules cover only campaign advertising, leaving out vast amounts of AI content from ordinary citizens and anonymous accounts, while misinformation laws face loopholes and intentionality burdens of proof.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Most election AI content falls outside formal rules—pressure shifts to platform moderation.

themes.theme: Scale of AI content in 2026 elections

insights.claim: In Israel's late-October 2026 general election, an estimated 1 in 8 election-related social media posts were altered by AI, including posts from Benjamin Netanyahu, Bezalel Smotrich, Itamar Ben-Gvir, and Gadi Eisenkot.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: AI-generated political content is now mainstream, not fringe—driving demand for detection and provenance tools.
insights.quote: an estimated 1 in 8 election-related social media posts altered by AI

insights.claim: Ahead of the November 3, 2026 US midterms, an estimated $137 million was spent on over 220 videos using AI-generated content, and about 70% lacked an AI disclosure.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Material political ad spend is flowing into AI video production, largely undisclosed.
insights.quote: an estimated $137 million has been spent on over 220 videos that use AI-generated content
insights.locator: Ahead of the U.S. midterm elections

insights.claim: In Colombia's May 2026 presidential election nearly all candidates used AI-generated videos, such as Pacto Histórico's Iván Cepeda using an animated refrigerator to back a minimum wage increase.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Shows normalization of AI campaign content across Latin America.

insights.claim: AI election content is created and spread not only by fringe or anonymous accounts but by political leaders and parties with funding and campaign infrastructure.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Mainstream adoption makes outright bans politically costly—favoring disclosure regimes.
insights.locator: In each of the countries highlighted

insights.claim: Online deepfakes were estimated to have increased from 500,000 in 2023 to 8 million in 2025 as generative AI lowered cost and technical barriers.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: 16x growth in two years underpins the market for deepfake detection and content-provenance tech.
insights.quote: Between 2023 and 2025, online deepfakes were estimated to have increased from 500,000 to 8 million.
insights.locator: Enforcing Regulation at the Speed of AI

insights.claim: Israel began requiring labels on AI-generated election content in July 2026 for material that 'could appear to have been authentically documented when it was not,' but critics note the test is perceived realism, not intent, so a labeled deception complies.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Disclosure-only regimes may provide legal cover for deceptive content rather than curbing it.

insights.claim: Israeli Justice Noam Sohlberg ordered Bezalel Smotrich to remove a labeled AI clip of Gadi Eisenkot shaking hands with Mahmoud Abbas because Facebook users would be unlikely to see the disclaimer, yet later refused to remove another Smotrich AI video, saying it was to be 'judged by the voters, not by election law.'
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Inconsistent judicial outcomes create unpredictable compliance risk for platforms.
insights.quote: judged by the voters, not by election law.
insights.locator: At the same time, even when labels

insights.claim: Spain approved a 2025 bill fining companies up to $38 million for not labeling AI content, yet the People's Party's AI video impersonating Pedro Sánchez's wife and Socialist figures carried a small, faint label that may still shield it legally.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Large fines exist on paper, but compliance can be minimal-effort—enforcement design matters more than fine size.

insights.claim: When distinguishing political expression from deception depends on judges' subjective interpretation, regulators risk influencing which political messages circulate.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Regulatory discretion over AI political speech is itself a political risk and a free-speech flashpoint.
insights.locator: Arguably, the recent Spanish and Israeli

themes.theme: Enforcement speed and the US patchwork

insights.claim: Enforcement lags virality: Spain's PP deepfake drew over 2 million views in under a day before legal complaints were filed, and Israeli rulings on Smotrich's videos came weeks after posting.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Takedown regimes are structurally too slow; real-time detection/provenance at platform level is the only effective lever.
insights.quote: generated over 2 million views across social media platforms in less than a day

insights.claim: The United States has no federal deepfake law; in 2024 the Federal Election Commission declined to create a separate AI rule, and the FAIR Elections Act proposed in June 2026 has not been enacted.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Federal AI-election regulation remains a pending policy risk/opportunity for AI and platform companies.
insights.quote: the United States has no federal law specifically addressing deepfakes

insights.claim: California, Maryland, Minnesota, and Texas ban political deepfakes for varying pre-election periods and 27 other states require disclosures; the authors argue this patchwork will be ineffective since AI content crosses state lines.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Patchwork compliance raises costs for platforms and may build pressure for federal preemption.
insights.quote: a patchwork approach will be ineffective
insights.locator: In the absence of a comprehensive

insights.claim: The authors conclude effective deepfake regulation depends less on what rules prohibit than on how effectively they can be enforced before Election Day.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Watch for timing-focused rules (pre-election blackout windows, rapid takedown mandates).
insights.quote: how effectively they can be enforced before Election Day
